title: 1 Chronicles 28:1–10
context: David gathers Israel’s leaders in Jerusalem and tells them he had wanted to build a house of rest for the ark, but God said he must not because he was a man of war, and chose Solomon to build it and sit on the throne of the LORD’s kingdom. David charges the assembly and Solomon to keep the LORD’s commandments, to serve God with a perfect heart and a willing mind, and to be strong and build. Both traditions read the charge as shared ground, and the promise recalls 2 Samuel 7 and 1 Chronicles 17, while the reason given for David not building differs in emphasis from 2 Samuel 7 and 1 Kings 5:3.

verses.text: David assembled all the princes of Israel, the princes of the tribes, the captains of the companies who served the king by division, the captains of thousands, the captains of hundreds, and the rulers over all the substance and possessions of the king and of his sons, with the officers and the mighty men, even all the mighty men of valor, to Jerusalem.
verses.arminianNotes:
David assembles “all the princes of Israel,” the tribal leaders, captains, officials, and mighty men in Jerusalem. Arminian readers note that the transfer of the temple project and the kingdom is made in public, before the whole leadership.

The Chronicler stresses the involvement of all Israel throughout these chapters.
verses.reformedNotes:
Reformed readers also see the public setting as significant: what God has purposed is announced before the people who will carry it out.

Both traditions treat this as shared ground: the work of God’s house is a shared calling, not the king’s private project.

verses.text: Then David the king stood up on his feet and said, “Hear me, my brothers and my people! As for me, it was in my heart to build a house of rest for the ark of the LORD’s covenant, and for the footstool of our God; and I had prepared for the building.
verses.arminianNotes:
David says it was in his heart “to build a house of rest for the ark of the LORD’s covenant, and for the footstool of our God” (cf. Ps 132:7). Arminian readers note his sincere desire to honor God.

He had already “prepared for the building” (cf. 1 Chr 22:2–5).
verses.reformedNotes:
Reformed readers see David’s desire as good, even though God redirects it.

Both traditions treat this as shared ground: the ark as God’s footstool pictures his rule from heaven, and David’s preparation shows devotion that serves a purpose beyond his own reign.

verses.text: But God said to me, ‘You shall not build a house for my name, because you are a man of war and have shed blood.’
verses.arminianNotes:
God said, “You shall not build a house for my name, because you are a man of war and have shed blood.” Arminian readers note that the reason is stated plainly, as in 1 Chronicles 22:8.

2 Samuel 7 gives no such reason, and 1 Kings 5:3 speaks of the wars that surrounded David; the books differ in emphasis.
verses.reformedNotes:
Reformed readers see God’s freedom to assign different tasks to different servants.

Both traditions treat this as shared ground: the reason does not cancel David’s faithfulness, and the parallels are read side by side without being harmonized.

verses.text: However the LORD, the God of Israel, chose me out of all the house of my father to be king over Israel forever. For he has chosen Judah to be prince; and in the house of Judah, the house of my father; and among the sons of my father he took pleasure in me to make me king over all Israel.
verses.arminianNotes:
David says, “However the LORD, the God of Israel, chose me out of all the house of my father to be king over Israel forever.” Arminian readers note that David traces his kingship to God’s choice, moving from Judah to his father’s house to himself.

This is a choice to a role and a covenant line (cf. Gen 49:10; 1 Sam 16:1–13).
verses.reformedNotes:
Reformed readers see God’s sovereign choice narrowing step by step from tribe to family to person.

Both traditions treat this as shared ground: the verse concerns God’s choice of a king and his dynasty, and it should not be pressed into the wider debate about election to salvation.

verses.text: Of all my sons (for the LORD has given me many sons), he has chosen Solomon my son to sit on the throne of the LORD’s kingdom over Israel.
verses.arminianNotes:
Of all his sons, “he has chosen Solomon my son to sit on the throne of the LORD’s kingdom over Israel.” Arminian readers note that the kingdom is called the LORD’s, not David’s.

The king rules as a steward under God.
verses.reformedNotes:
Reformed readers see the same emphasis: the throne belongs to the LORD, and Solomon sits on it by God’s choice.

Both traditions treat this as shared ground, and the phrase prepares for 29:23, where Solomon sits “on the throne of the LORD.”

verses.text: He said to me, ‘Solomon, your son, shall build my house and my courts; for I have chosen him to be my son, and I will be his father.
verses.arminianNotes:
God said, “Solomon, your son, shall build my house and my courts; for I have chosen him to be my son, and I will be his father.” Arminian readers note the echo of 2 Samuel 7:13–14 and 1 Chronicles 17:12–13.

The father-son language is covenant language for the king.
verses.reformedNotes:
Reformed readers likewise hear the promise to David’s offspring, which the New Testament applies to Christ (Heb 1:5).

Both traditions treat this as shared ground, consistent with the notes on 2 Samuel 7: a historical fulfillment in Solomon and a fuller fulfillment in Christ.

verses.text: I will establish his kingdom forever if he continues to do my commandments and my ordinances, as it is today.’
verses.arminianNotes:
“I will establish his kingdom forever if he continues to do my commandments and my ordinances, as it is today.” Arminian readers note that the “if” is a real condition for Solomon’s own reign.

The promise and the call to obedience stand together, as in 1 Kings 2:4.
verses.reformedNotes:
Reformed readers also refuse to erase the condition, while holding that God’s promise to David’s line does not ultimately fail.

Both traditions treat this as shared ground, as in the notes on 1 Kings 2:4: God’s word is sure, and the king is called to faithfulness.

verses.text: Now therefore, in the sight of all Israel, the LORD’s assembly, and in the audience of our God, observe and seek out all the commandments of the LORD your God, that you may possess this good land, and leave it for an inheritance to your children after you forever.
verses.arminianNotes:
Before “all Israel, the LORD’s assembly,” David charges them to “observe and seek out all the commandments of the LORD your God, that you may possess this good land.” Arminian readers note the link between obedience and continued life in the land.

The charge echoes Deuteronomy.
verses.reformedNotes:
Reformed readers see the covenant pattern of gift and obligation: the land is God’s gift, and obedience is the fitting response.

Both traditions treat this as shared ground: the charge looks ahead to the children who will inherit the land.

verses.text: You, Solomon my son, know the God of your father, and serve him with a perfect heart and with a willing mind; for the LORD searches all hearts, and understands all the imaginations of the thoughts. If you seek him, he will be found by you; but if you forsake him, he will cast you off forever.
verses.arminianNotes:
David tells Solomon to “serve him with a perfect heart and with a willing mind; for the LORD searches all hearts.” Arminian readers note that David calls Solomon to wholehearted service, and that God sees beyond outward appearances (cf. 1 Sam 16:7).

“If you seek him, he will be found by you” (cf. 2 Chr 15:2).
verses.reformedNotes:
Reformed readers also hear the call to wholehearted service and the reminder that God knows every thought (cf. Jer 17:10).

Both traditions treat this as shared ground: the warning “if you forsake him, he will cast you off forever” is serious, and both read it as a real call to seek God.

verses.text: Take heed now, for the LORD has chosen you to build a house for the sanctuary. Be strong, and do it.”
verses.arminianNotes:
“Take heed now, for the LORD has chosen you to build a house for the sanctuary. Be strong, and do it.” Arminian readers note that God’s choice calls for Solomon’s active response.

The charge recalls Joshua’s commission (Josh 1:6–9).
verses.reformedNotes:
Reformed readers see God’s choice as the ground of Solomon’s confidence and effort.

Both traditions treat this as shared ground: being chosen for a task brings the responsibility to take it up with courage.
